title: ACS Lecture 1: Processor Evolution — From CPU to GPU

notes.title: Course Introduction and Key Question
notes.summary: The lecture asks why AI computing shifted from CPU-centric to GPU-centric systems, and lays out a roadmap from code execution and host machines to CPU/GPU microarchitecture, parallel programming models, and AI performance models.
notes.detail: The stated path begins with review material on how code runs and completes computation and what a host machine looks like, then moves to core CPU vs GPU microarchitecture, parallel programming models, and a performance model for AI workloads. Readings include Hennessy & Patterson (CACM 2019), Dally, Keckler & Kirk (IEEE Micro 2021), Williams, Waterman & Patterson (CACM 2009), and Dao et al., FlashAttention (NeurIPS 2022).
keyPoints: Key question: why did AI computing move from CPU-centric to GPU-centric systems?
Roadmap starts with review of how code runs and completes computation
Then reviews what a host machine looks like
Core topics: CPU vs GPU microarchitecture, parallel programming models, AI workload performance model
Readings span computer architecture, GPU evolution, Roofline, and FlashAttention

notes.title: Transformation Hierarchy of Computing
notes.summary: Writing Y = Model(X) triggers a chain from algorithm design through program, system software, OS scheduling, and hardware execution, returning result Y to the application.
notes.detail: The workflow begins by designing an algorithm Model with input data X, then a program expresses that algorithm. System software turns the program into an executable, parallel, robust task, the OS schedules and deploys tasks onto hardware, and hardware executes instructions and moves data to produce Y.
keyPoints: Step 1: design an algorithm Model to solve a problem with input data X
Step 2: a program expresses the algorithm
Step 3: system software turns the program into an executable, parallel, and robust task
Step 4: the OS schedules computing tasks and deploys them onto hardware; hardware executes instructions and moves data
Step 5: computation completes and result Y is returned to the application

topics.title: Host Architecture and Roles in AI Computing

notes.title: Host System Components and Motherboard Integration
notes.summary: A modern host system connects CPU, DDR/DRAM, GPU/accelerator, SSD/storage, NIC/network and PCIe/interconnect, with end-to-end performance depending on how these are interconnected.
notes.detail: The host is presented as an execution platform built from CPUs with their DDRs and caches, memory controllers, PCIe switches (PIX, 5.0, 512Gbps), GPUs linked by NV-Link at 450GB/s, and a 200Gbps link between the PCIe and NV-Link domains. The motherboard acts as the integration plane where CPU, DDR, GPU, NVLink, SSD/NVMe, NIC and PCIe come together.
keyPoints: Components listed: CPU, DDR/DRAM, GPU/accelerator, SSD/storage, NIC/network, PCIe/interconnect.
CPUs pair with DDRs and multi-level caches (Level Cache, Last Level Cache) via memory controllers.
PCIe switches are labeled PIX, 5.0, 512Gbps; NV-Link is labeled 450GB/s.
A 200Gbps link connects the PCIe side to the NV-Link/GPU side.
Key lesson: end-to-end performance depends on the interconnection.

notes.title: Roles of CPU, GPU, and NIC in AI Computing
notes.summary: The CPU acts as host controller running the OS and orchestrating data flow, the GPU supplies high-throughput matrix computation, and the NIC scales one system into distributed computing across many hosts.
notes.detail: The CPU installs system software (e.g., Debian/CentOS), acts as the PCIe root, monitors power and temperature, and prepares input data from SSD/DRAM before calling GPU kernels; the GPU performs matrix/tensor operations with HBM for maximum efficiency, and the NIC connects many hosts to execute the same task.
keyPoints: CPU: runs OS/system software, manages devices, and launches Python frameworks for inference/training
GPU: handles matrix and tensor operations, packaging HBM for maximum computation efficiency
NIC: scales a single computing system for distributed computing, e.g., 5D parallelism (Lecture 9)
A host server typically holds eight GPUs, limited by power supply and heat dissipation
A training task may involve thousands of servers needing a high-bandwidth network (Lecture 5)

notes.title: CUDA Host-Device Execution Model
notes.summary: CUDA execution flows Host → Device → Network → Device → Host, with the CPU managing memory, data copies, kernel launches and synchronization while the GPU runs many threads to execute kernels.
notes.detail: The host side (CPU) allocates memory, copies data, launches kernels and performs synchronization; the device side (GPU) runs many threads to execute kernels. The overall path is Host -> Device -> Network -> Device -> Host.
keyPoints: Host side is the CPU; device side is the GPU.
CPU responsibilities: allocate memory, copy data, launch kernels, synchronization.
GPU responsibility: run many threads to execute kernels.
Data path spans host, device and network in both directions.

notes.title: Instruction Execution and CPU Architecture Overview
notes.summary: Instruction execution is the last step of computing, comprising load from RAM to register file, compute among registers, and store back to RAM, and its efficiency determines maximum computing power and speed.
notes.detail: A computing core has three components: ALU for computing, register file for data load/store, and instruction memory for pipelining. The Intel Xeon 6980P example shows 256 threads deciding parallelism, 3.2GHz deciding ALU/instruction execution speed, and 504MB cache deciding data load/store speed.
keyPoints: Load: from RAM to register file.
Compute: add, mul among registers.
Store: from register file to RAM.
Core components: ALU (computing), register file (load/store), instruction memory (pipelining).
CPU optimizes latency of a small number of complex threads.

notes.title: Five-Stage Instruction Pipeline and Hazards
notes.summary: The five-stage pipeline overlaps instruction execution across IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB stages to hide data load/store time, but hazards cause stalls and bubbles.
notes.detail: A perfect pipeline completes one instruction per cycle after filling, giving Total Cycles = M + N – 1 for N instructions and M stages. Any condition that stalls the pipeline is a hazard: data hazards arise from dependencies (RAW, WAW, WAR) and control hazards from branches, whose penalty worsens with deeper pipelines and whose uncertainty grows with branchy code.
keyPoints: Stages: Fetch (IF), Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), Write Back (WB)
Perfect pipeline: one instruction completes per cycle after filling, no bubbles
Data hazards: RAW, WAW, WAR dependencies
Control hazards: deeper pipeline causes worse penalty; branches create uncertainty

notes.title: Pipeline Optimizations: Data Forwarding and Register Renaming
notes.summary: Data forwarding passes results directly from pipeline registers to ALU inputs so consumers execute earlier, while register renaming uses more registers to decouple dependencies.
notes.detail: Forwarding enables register-to-register or register-to-ALU paths, letting the consumer execute earlier and yielding fewer stalls and higher pipeline efficiency. Register renaming uses more registers to decouple dependencies, and the lecture illustrates both techniques with worked examples.
keyPoints: Forwarding: result passed directly from pipeline register to ALU input
Consumer can execute earlier → fewer stalls, higher pipeline efficiency
Register renaming: more registers decouple dependencies

notes.title: Advanced CPU Optimizations: OoO, Superscalar, Speculative Execution, Hyper-Threading
notes.summary: OoO execution, superscalar issue, speculative execution with branch prediction, and hyper-threading each attack idle slots and stalls to raise latency and throughput.
notes.detail: OoO separates program order, execution order and commit order, with the compiler typically finding independent instruction sets to reduce stall time. Superscalar tries to execute multiple instructions per cycle via a wide pipeline (wide fetch/decode, multiple execution units, load/store paths, writeback, multi-ported register file), while speculative execution issues risky instructions for quick completion and a busy deep pipeline at the cost of wasted wrong-path work and recovery penalties; hyper-threading adds SMT so multiple hardware threads share one physical core.
keyPoints: OoO separates program order, execution order, and commit order
Superscalar needs a wide pipeline: wide fetch/decode, multiple execution units and load/store paths, wide writeback, multi-ported register file
Speculation benefit: low latency and high throughput; cost: wasted energy/cycles and recovery penalty growing with pipeline depth
Branch prediction: naïve static prediction lets the compiler remove not-taken branches; dynamic prediction also exists
Hyper-threading (SMT): multiple hardware threads share one physical core, each with its own architectural state

notes.title: CPU Optimization Summary
notes.summary: A modern CPU core spends many transistors on data forwarding, register renaming, OoO execution, superscalar and speculative execution to optimize latency for a small number of complex threads.
notes.detail: These optimizations target latency of a small number of complex threads; ideal scenarios include control-heavy programs, irregular data structures, OS and runtime services, and low-latency request handling.
keyPoints: Optimizations listed: data forwarding, register renaming, OoO execution, superscalar, speculative execution
Ideal for control-heavy programs
Ideal for irregular data structures
Ideal for OS and runtime services
Ideal for low-latency request handling

notes.title: From CPU to GPU: Parallelism and Multiprocessors
notes.summary: Throughput scaling moves beyond a single superscalar core by using many cores with a memory hierarchy, many servers with networking, and explicit parallelism.
notes.detail: A superscalar core reaches its ceiling through high frequency, deep pipeline and minimal hazards, so scaling means adding superscalar cores with memory hierarchy and servers with networking. Parallelism is data parallelism (vector and array processing) or task parallelism (multithreading); CPU scales to hundreds of heavy cores for control, GPU to 1,000s–10,000s of light cores for compute.
keyPoints: Single superscalar core ceiling: high frequency, deep pipeline, minimal hazards
Scale cores with memory hierarchy; scale servers with networking
Data parallelism: different pieces of data in parallel (vector/array processing)
Task parallelism: different tasks in parallel (multithreading)
CPU: control logic and dependencies cause synchronization, so hundreds of heavy cores; GPU: less control logic, easy data parallelism, so 1,000s–10,000s of light cores, 10x–100x CPU computing power

notes.title: GPU Chip Organization and CUDA Programming Model
notes.summary: A GPU chip has hundreds of streaming multiprocessors (SMs), each with processing units, a warp scheduler and shared memory, programmed via CUDA's kernel, thread block, warp and thread hierarchy.
notes.detail: Each SM contains simplified pipelines for specific precisions (INT32, FP32, FP64), a warp scheduler that packages threads into warps and switches to a ready warp when one waits, and high-speed shared memory for intra-SM exchange. A thread block is assigned to one SM (up to 8 blocks per SM; Fermi SM up to 1536 threads, e.g. 256*6 or 512*3 blocks), each block divided into 32-thread warps under SIMT, where threads in a warp should execute the same code but may take different branches.
keyPoints: CUDA hierarchy: kernel = GPU-level jobs, thread block = SM-level jobs, warp = minimal executing unit, thread = operator
SM units execute specific instructions for specific computing precision with simplified pipelines
Warp scheduler picks which warp runs per time slot; threads share a register file; when one warp waits, another ready warp is scheduled
Thread block assigned to one SM, up to 8 blocks per SM; Fermi SM up to 1536 threads
SIMT: threads in a warp should execute same instructions, but different branches are allowed

notes.title: SIMD Execution and Warp Execution
notes.summary: SMs act as SIMD units, issuing one instruction per thread per clock, and warp execution interleaves warps to hide latencies.
notes.detail: The SM's SIMD pipeline executes one instruction per thread, per clock, and the control unit is shared by multiple processing units/SIMD pipelines. Interleaving execution among warps hides latencies.
keyPoints: SIMD pipeline: one instruction per thread, per clock
Control unit shared by multiple processing units / SIMD pipelines
Interleave execution among warps to hide latencies
Vector length is called warp size (NVIDIA) or wavefront size (AMD)

notes.title: CPU vs GPU Architecture Comparison
notes.summary: CPUs use a few heavy out-of-order superscalar hyper-threading cores, while GPUs use many light in-order SIMD-pipeline cores to enable thousands of threads.
notes.detail: The CPU is described as a few out-of-order, superscalar, hyper-threading cores — heavy cores. The GPU instead has many in-order, SIMD-pipeline cores — light cores — enabling 1,000 to 10,000 threads for parallel computing.
keyPoints: CPU: few out-of-order, superscalar, hyper-threading cores (heavy)
GPU: many in-order, SIMD-pipeline cores (light)
GPU enables 1,000 to 10,000 threads for parallel computing

notes.title: Control Divergence and SIMD Utilization
notes.summary: Control divergence occurs when threads in a warp branch to different paths, so only a subset executes and SIMD pipeline utilization is wasted.
notes.detail: A GPU uses a SIMD pipeline to save area on control logic and groups scalar threads into warps; branch divergence arises when threads inside warps branch to different execution paths. Divergence-free programs increase SIMD utilization, and in vector reduction the optimized program keeps all active threads in the same warp.
keyPoints: SIMD pipeline saves area on control logic
Branch divergence: threads inside warps take different execution paths
Result: only a subset of threads execute, wasting SIMD utilization
Divergence-free programs increase SIMD utilization
Optimized vector reduction keeps all active threads in the same warp

notes.title: Atomic Operations and Histogram Calculation
notes.summary: Atomic operations are required when threads update the same memory location, and histogram calculation can be optimized with per-block sub-histograms.
notes.detail: CUDA provides int atomicAdd(int*, int); atomic conflicts are measured as the number of threads in a warp that update the same memory position. Histograms count data instances in disjoint bins, and optimized histogram calculation uses per-block sub-histograms.
keyPoints: Atomic operations required when threads update the same memory location
CUDA: int atomicAdd (int*, int)
Atomic conflicts: number of threads in a warp updating the same memory position
Histograms count data instances in disjoint categories (bins)
Optimized histogram calculation uses per-block sub-histograms

notes.title: Why AI Moved Toward GPU-Centric Computing
notes.summary: Scaling laws made compute the bottleneck and Transformers made computation massively data-parallel, so the hardware target shifted to high-throughput training on GPUs rather than low-latency single-thread execution.
notes.detail: Empirical loss improves predictably as compute, parameters, and data increase, scaling model size and token count together. Transformers expose SIMD/SIMT-friendly work in dense tensor kernels, with the CPU remaining host controller while the GPU becomes the dominant floating-point compute engine.
keyPoints: Scaling laws turn AI into sustained FLOP demand, making compute the bottleneck.
Transformers expose SIMD/SIMT-friendly work across parallel axes: batch, token, head, hidden dimension.
Most expensive layers are dense tensor kernels: QKV projection, QK^T attention scores, AV product, FFN GEMM.
Control flow is small and arithmetic intensity is high when tiled well.
GPU-centric execution means many simple threads plus high bandwidth and tensor units.

topics.title: Parallel Programming Models: pThread and CUDA

notes.title: CPU Multicore Programming with pThread
notes.summary: pThread breaks a complex task into lightweight threads within one process that share the virtual address space, so global variables and heap objects are shared and synchronization is the programmer's job.
notes.detail: The pThread library (POSIX threads) is a standard for Unix-like systems linked with C/C++ programs; the example uses a fork-join pattern that partitions input into per-thread chunks for a parallel reduction. Because threads share memory, concurrent updates like sum += local_sum can race: each thread loads, adds and stores, so one write may overwrite another.
keyPoints: One process contains multiple threads sharing the same virtual address space.
Global variables and heap objects are shared across threads.
Synchronization is the programmer's responsibility.
pThread is a POSIX standard for Unix-like OSes, linked with C/C++ programs.
Fork-join pattern partitions input into per-thread chunks.

notes.title: Synchronization Primitives: Mutex, Barriers, Condition Variables
notes.summary: A mutex serializes access to a critical section so only one thread at a time updates protected shared state, while barriers and condition variables coordinate thread progress and waiting.
notes.detail: The mutex pattern wraps the critical section in pthread_mutex_lock and pthread_mutex_unlock, giving race avoidance for protected shared state at the cost of lock contention, since other threads wait while one holds the lock. A barrier makes all threads wait until everyone reaches the same point, and a condition variable lets a thread sleep until a condition becomes true.
keyPoints: Mutex provides serialized access to the critical section and race avoidance for protected shared state.
Cost of a mutex is lock contention: only one thread holds it, others wait and the region is serialized.
Barrier: all threads wait until everyone reaches the same point; used in phase-based algorithms, debugging and iterative solvers.
Condition variable: a thread sleeps until a condition becomes true; used in worker pools and event-driven scheduling.

notes.title: From pThread to CUDA: Same Idea, Different Granularity
notes.summary: Both pThread and CUDA divide work across parallel workers, but CUDA makes each worker much smaller and far more numerous than pThread's coarse OS threads.
notes.detail: pThread uses a few OS threads handling coarse tasks, while CUDA uses many logical threads each mapped to a data element, following the same SIMD/SIMT pattern. The work unit and launch API differ: pthread_create/pthread_join versus CUDA thread/data element and kernel launch.
keyPoints: pThread: few OS threads, coarse tasks
CUDA: many logical threads, data elements
Same SIMD/SIMT pattern underlies both models
Work unit differs: OS thread/task vs CUDA thread/data element

notes.title: CUDA Program Structure, Kernel Definition, and Synchronization
notes.summary: CUDA starts on the CPU: host code allocates device memory, copies data, launches the kernel asynchronously, and copies results back.
notes.detail: The host uses cudaMalloc and cudaMemcpy to move h_A/h_B to d_A/d_B, launches vecAdd<<<numBlocks, blockSize>>>, then copies d_C back to h_C. Because kernel launch is asynchronous, cudaDeviceSynchronize() or a blocking copy is needed.
keyPoints: Host manages device memory, data movement, and kernel launch
Kernel launch is asynchronous; synchronize before using results
Kernel index: i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x, guarded by if (i < n)
__syncthreads() scope is one CUDA block, used for shared-memory tile coordination
Kernel boundary synchronizes all threads, achieved by launching separate kernels

notes.title: Performance Is Not Peak FLOPs
notes.summary: Real performance is bounded by hardware throughput but limited below peak by load imbalance, pipeline efficiency, and memory access.
notes.detail: Speedup is computed as T(1)/T(P) with P cores, and efficiency as Speedup/P. Both speedup and efficiency usually vary with problem size and the number of involved cores.
keyPoints: Hardware throughput is only an upper bound
Load imbalance, pipeline efficiency, and memory access limit real performance
Speedup and efficiency vary with problem size and core count

notes.title: Amdahl's Law
notes.summary: When problem size is fixed, even a small serial fraction caps total speedup, since more processors only squeeze the parallelizable part.
notes.detail: With parallelizable fraction f and serial fraction 1-f, adding processors reduces the parallel term f/p but the serial part remains. Numerically, f=0.90 caps speedup near 10x and f=0.99 near 100x.
keyPoints: Fixed problem size assumption
Serial fraction 1-f remains regardless of processor count
f=0.90 gives max speedup about 10x; f=0.99 about 100x

notes.title: Roofline Model
notes.summary: The Roofline model uses arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte moved from memory) to decide whether a kernel is limited by memory bandwidth or by compute capability.
notes.detail: Arithmetic Intensity is defined as FLOPs divided by bytes moved from memory. A kernel is memory-bound when limited by bandwidth times intensity, and compute-bound when it still needs vectorization, tensor cores and occupancy to reach peak.
keyPoints: Arithmetic Intensity = FLOPs / Bytes moved from memory
Memory-bound: limited by bandwidth x intensity
Compute-bound: still needs vectorization, tensor cores, occupancy
Real ceilings fall with poor locality or pipeline utilization
